summary:
La Rioja stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the Law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGBTI persons, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE no. 51, 1 March 2023), applies uniformly across the autonomous communities, including this one. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route that replaces the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment; Title II allows adults to rectify the registered sex marker by simple declaration and provides for corresponding document adaptation, and transitory provisions govern applications pending at entry into force.

The same law mandates public-policy, workplace, health and education measures, regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and permits recognition from age 12 under conditions, a provision Human Rights Watch reported as contentious. It also prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing, and bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before they can consent.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the Civil Registry is the operative basis for facility rules.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Courts apply the aggravation in practice: a Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300, while in Valencia a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, with two minors judged separately.

La Rioja's own regional trans-rights law of February 2022 already allowed trans people to self-declare their legal gender and granted protective rights to trans visitors and residents, so the national framework layers onto an existing permissive regional base rather than replacing restriction; the regional law remains in force alongside the national Ley Trans.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied across Spain since 2005, and Spain is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch frames the 28 February 2023 reform as bringing Spain's legal gender recognition into line with European and international standards that reject disproportionate requirements, and places the country alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay in using administrative self-declaration.

Adjacent reforms carried by Ley 4/2023, of limited direct bearing on a trans visitor's own position, include expanded access to assisted reproduction, strengthened sexuality education, and parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples.

La Rioja created its same-sex couple registry in 2010, five years after same-sex marriage and adoption rights took effect nationally in 2005, and is listed among the autonomous communities that ban conversion therapies.
localsOnly:
Residents of La Rioja have been able to self-declare their legal gender under the regional trans-rights law of February 2022, which continues to apply alongside Ley 4/2023 and granted protective rights to trans people living in the community.

Applications for rectification already pending when Ley 4/2023 entered into force are handled under its transitory provisions, and the corresponding adaptation of identity documents follows the administrative route rather than a medical one.

The regional law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16 and allows recognition from age 12 under conditions, which is where parental and clinical decision-making sits for residents.

La Rioja is listed among the autonomous communities banning conversion therapies, a measure that binds practitioners within the community.
outOfScopeNotes:
No La Rioja-specific enforcement data appears in the source inventory: there is no reported case from the community illustrating how the transfobia aggravation at Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code or the Article 510 hate-speech offence has been applied locally, and the two documented cases come from Vigo and Valencia in other communities.

Whether the Civil Registry offices serving La Rioja handle Article 43 applications with the same processing times or evidentiary practice as elsewhere in Spain is not sourced here.

The conditions attached to recognition from age 12, and the precise scope of the 12-to-16 consent rules, are not set out in the available sources beyond the statement that they exist and proved contentious.

The conversion-therapy ban and the 2010 same-sex couple registry are sourced to an encyclopaedic page citing an LGBT federation release, not to the text of the regional statutes themselves; verification against the published regional law remains outstanding.

No source in the inventory addresses practical conditions of facility access, identification screening at borders or airports, or documentation of trans travellers entering La Rioja.
